intro: Nineteen verses of lament that never turns. The psalm opens in the dark and its last word is darkness, and unlike every other lament in the book it offers no thanks, no vow and no rescue at the end. It is the best page here for the second person perfect, because almost every complaint is a verb ending in -ta, You have: You put me, You have removed, You have afflicted. The superscription carries two attributions and two musical terms nobody can now translate with confidence. Read it slowly and let it stay unresolved, because that is what it is.

stichs.en: A song, a psalm of the sons of Korah;
for the leader, upon Mahalath Leannoth;
a maskil of Heman the Ezrahite.

verses.summary: One of the longest superscriptions in the book, and it names two owners: the Korah singers and Heman the Ezrahite. Two of its words are directions for performance whose meaning is lost.

stichs.en: LORD, God of my salvation,
by day I have cried out, in the night, before You.

verses.summary: The only good thing the psalm says about God, and it is said in the vocative. Salvation is the address, not the experience being reported.

stichs.en: Let my prayer come before You;
incline Your ear to my cry.

verses.summary: Two requests, and they are the last requests in the psalm. Everything from verse 4 onward is description rather than asking.

stichs.en: For my soul is full of troubles,
and my life has come to the edge of Sheol.

verses.summary: The verb of the second half is one of arrival, not of danger. Sheol is not what threatens the speaker; it is the place he reports having reached.

stichs.en: I am counted with those who go down to the pit;
I have become like a man with no strength.

verses.summary: The speaker is now a member of a group rather than an individual in trouble. Both verbs are passive or stative: nothing here is something he does.

stichs.en: Among the dead, set loose,
like the slain who lie in the grave,
whom You remember no longer,
and they are cut off from Your hand.

verses.summary: The hardest phrase in the psalm sits at the start: free among the dead, where freedom means released from being remembered. The one doing the forgetting is God.

stichs.en: You have put me in the lowest pit,
in dark places, in the depths.

verses.summary: Three locations in five words, all of them below, and the verb is second person. The pit is not where the speaker fell; it is where he was placed.

stichs.en: Your wrath has leaned hard upon me,
and with all Your breaking waves You have brought me down. Selah.

verses.summary: Wrath is described as weight resting on a body, then as surf. The sea image here does not flood the speaker from outside; it holds him under.

stichs.en: You have put my friends far from me,
You have made me a horror to them;
I am shut in and cannot go out.

verses.summary: Isolation is reported as an act of God rather than as an effect of illness. The final clause is the shortest sentence in the psalm and the most physical.

stichs.en: My eye has wasted away from affliction;
I have called You, LORD, every day,
I have spread out my palms to You.

verses.summary: The verse that keeps this a prayer rather than a report. Whatever has stopped, the calling has not, and the open palms are the posture of someone still expecting.

stichs.en: Will You do a wonder for the dead?
Will the shades rise and thank You? Selah.

glosses: is it for the dead that
verses.summary: The first of three interrogative markers that carry six questions across three verses. The argument underneath them is practical: praise requires a living mouth.

stichs.en: Is Your kindness told in the grave,
Your faithfulness in the place of ruin?

verses.summary: The two nouns are the pair the psalter uses for what God can be relied on to be. The question is whether they have any audience in the grave.

stichs.en: Is Your wonder known in the dark,
and Your righteousness in the land of forgetting?

verses.summary: The last name given to death here is the land of forgetting. The question is not whether the dead survive but whether anything of God is known where they are.

stichs.en: But I have cried to You for help, LORD,
and in the morning my prayer comes to meet You.

verses.summary: The place where a lament usually turns. Morning arrives and the prayer is early, and then nothing follows from it: the next verse asks why.

stichs.en: Why, LORD, do You cast off my soul?
Why do You hide Your face from me?

verses.summary: The only why in the psalm, and it is asked of God directly. Hidden face is the standing phrase for the absence of someone who has not gone anywhere.

stichs.en: I am afflicted and dying from my youth;
I have carried Your terrors, I am numb.

verses.summary: Suffering is given a duration and it is a lifetime, not a recent blow. The last word of the verse occurs nowhere else in the Bible and its meaning is genuinely unknown.

stichs.en: Your burning angers have passed over me;
Your terrors have destroyed me.

verses.summary: Both subjects are plural and both belong to God by suffix. Nothing in the verse is attributed to enemies, to fate or to chance.

stichs.en: They surround me like water all the day;
they close in on me together.

verses.summary: The waves of verse 8 return as a siege. The two adverbs, all the day and together, remove any interval in which to breathe.

stichs.en: You have put lover and friend far from me;
my companions are darkness.

verses.summary: The psalm ends where verse 9 began, with the friends removed, and the last word is darkness. No consolation is offered and none is implied.

pardes.body: Three cycles, each starting with an address to God and sliding back down. Verses 2 to 8 move from God of my salvation to the deeps; verses 9 to 13 move from isolation to the land of forgetting; verses 14 to 19 move from a prayer that arrives in the morning to a last word of darkness. Count the names for the underworld as you go, because the psalm collects them: Sheol, the pit, the grave, the depths, Abaddon, the dark, the land of forgetting. Notice too that the requests stop at verse 3. After that the psalm asks nothing and only reports, which is why it feels different from every other lament in the book.

Three cruxes worth knowing. {{16.6}}, the last word of verse 16, occurs nowhere else in the Bible; translations render it distracted, numb, or helpless, and the honest position is that it is unknown. {{1.6}} and {{1.7}} in the superscription are performance directions of contested meaning, variously read as an instrument, a melody name, or a manner of singing, and no reading is secure. {{6.1}}, free among the dead, is a phrase that reads as a benefit and functions as the opposite: the freedom in question is being released from God's memory, which the verse then restates as being cut off from His hand. {{11.4}}, the shades, is the standard biblical word for the dead as a class, and here they are asked whether they could rise and give thanks.

What the tradition did with this psalm is mostly that it kept it. It sits in the Korahite collection unsoftened, and the doxology that follows the next psalm belongs to the closing of the third book of the Psalter rather than to any resolution of these nineteen verses. One well established rabbinic reading turns {{6.1}} inside out: free among the dead becomes the source of the idea that the dead are released from the commandments, so that a phrase written as abandonment is heard as exemption. Read that way, the psalm's worst line becomes the tradition's technical term for what death changes, which is a fair example of how a lament is absorbed without being answered.

The psalm can be read as a description of concealment rather than of punishment. Verse 15 names it exactly: the face is hidden, not withdrawn, and everything else in the psalm follows from a presence that is entirely there and entirely unavailable. In the kabbalistic vocabulary this is the state in which the light is present but the vessel receives nothing, and the questions of verses 11 to 13 are then not rhetorical but structural: they ask whether the flow reaches the place where nothing is remembered. The psalm gives no answer, and {{19.5}}, its last word, leaves the reader inside the condition rather than outside describing it.
